spain.organisation: Compulsory service under the law of 29 June 1911: total 18 years — 3 in the active army (generally reduced to 2), 3 in the first reserve, 6 in the second reserve, the remainder in an (as yet unorganised) territorial reserve. Metropolitan Spain was divided into 8 territorial districts, each under a Captain-General; districts I-VI each furnished 2 field divisions, districts VII-VIII one each (14 infantry divisions in all). A division comprised 2 infantry brigades of 2 regiments of 3 battalions (third battalion a cadre only in peace), 1 cavalry regiment, 1 field artillery regiment of 5 batteries, and 1 engineer regiment; batteries had 4 guns. Additional troops: 3 independent chasseur (cazador) brigades of 6 battalions, 4 mountain artillery regiments (14 batteries), 1 horse artillery regiment (5 batteries), 1 permanent cavalry division (2 brigades) and 3 permanent cavalry brigades. Wartime field army about 220,000 combatants. Second line: 116 infantry, 14 cavalry and 14 artillery cadres for 7 reserve divisions (~90,000). Guardia Civil (<20,000) and Carabineros (~15,000) were military-disciplined constabulary/customs corps. Infantry weapon: Mauser Model 1893, 7 mm (calibre .275); field gun: Schneider Canet 14.5-pdr.
spain.garrisons: Distribution table (battalions/regiments, source SYB1913 p.1261): Spain 58 line infantry regiments, 15 chasseur battalions, 28 cavalry regiments, 18 field artillery, 7 horse/mountain, 6 garrison/siege; Africa (Melilla/Ceuta) 4, 2, 1, 1, 2, 1; Balearic Islands 4, 2, -, 1, -, 1; Canary Islands 4, 3, -, 1, -, 1. Totals 70 infantry regiments, 23 chasseur battalions, 29 cavalry, 19 field artillery, 13 other artillery, 7 fortress. The Army of Africa (Melilla, Ceuta, Larache, Alcazar) was nominally always on a war footing: corps of occupation of 12,000-15,000 combatants (4 infantry regiments of 3 battalions, 3 cazador battalions of 6 companies, 1 cavalry regiment of 6 squadrons, 3 field batteries, 3-4 mountain batteries, 1 howitzer battery, 1 engineer regiment, native infantry/cavalry and police units). During 1913-14 the Rif War absorbed most Spanish field troops; WWI1916 states 75,000 troops (~60% of the army) were in Morocco at the outbreak of war in August 1914. Fortresses guarded the Pyrenees and Portuguese frontier (Pasajes, Santoña, Santander, Ferrol, A Coruña, Vigo, Tarifa, Algeciras, Cádiz).
uncertainties: The 128,073 figure is a peace ESTABLISHMENT including two paramilitary corps; the number of effectives actually present under arms in January 1914 is not separately given and was certainly somewhat lower.

The 1913 edition of the SYB is the closest accessible contemporary publication; the 1914 edition could not be located online. The conscription/establishment law did not change before July 1914, so the figures are treated as valid for January 1914, but this is an inference.

The 90,000 reserve figure is what could be organised into 7 second-line divisions; the total pool of men with reserve liability under the 1911 law was larger but unquantified and, for the territorial reserve, unorganised.
The 220,000 field army and the 75,000-in-Morocco figures are mobilisation/war-crisis numbers (July-August 1914 onward) and must not be used as January 1914 peace strengths.
WORLDARMY is a secondary compilation; SYB1913 and WWI1916 are preferred for numbers.

active.reference_date: Peace establishment 'fixed of late years' as reported in 1913; applicable to January 1914 (1911 militia reorganisation in force; no mobilisation before 1916)
active.definition: PEACE ESTABLISHMENT of the metropolitan active (first-line) army: '30,000 men', with 'about 2,800 officers, all told' counted separately by the source. This is the establishment of the conscript militia-style active army, not a verified daily headcount of effectives. Excluded: Republican Guard (~5,000), Fiscal Guard (~5,200), colonial army (~10,150) and the reserve/territorial categories. Portugal was neutral and unmobilised in January 1914.
active.derivation: Direct reading of the SYB statement 'The peace establishment of the active army has been fixed of late years at 30,000 men. There are about 2,800 officers, all told.' The 30,000 is used as the active strength to avoid doubling the officers, whose relationship to the 30,000 is ambiguous in the text.
divergences: If the ~2,800 officers are additional to the 30,000 men, the total active army under arms would be about 32,800 — the source's wording is ambiguous.

HCPT gives about 44,000 'with colours including National Republican Guard and Police', plus about 10,000 in the colonies — a much broader definition that folds in paramilitary gendarmerie and colonial troops.

SYB1913 gives the broader structure (35 infantry regiments of 3 battalions, 11 cavalry regiments, 8 field artillery regiments with 63 batteries, etc.); Wikipedia (WIKI) describes the 1911 reform as 8 active divisions of 4 infantry regiments each plus a cavalry brigade — the same order of battle described at different levels, not a contradiction in numbers.

Portugal was not strictly a non-belligerent in practice after 1914 (seizure of German ships, border fighting in Africa from August 1914, war declared by Germany March 1916), but none of this affects the January 1914 peace establishment.

reserves.reference_date: Contemporary estimate of October 1914 (NYT1914), applied approximately to the 1914 reserve system in being in January 1914
reserves.definition: ESTIMATED trained reservists available in addition to the active army: the NYT (29 Oct 1914) reported about 130,000 'fully trained men in the active army and its two reserves' after wastage; subtracting the ~30,000-man active peace establishment gives roughly 100,000 trained reservists. This is an ESTIMATE by derivation, not a figure stated directly in the sources, and it is a mobilisation-availability figure — reservists were not under arms in January 1914. A further ~50,000 men of the territorial reserve were only partly trained and are excluded here.
reserves.derivation: 130,000 (active + two reserves, fully trained, after wastage) minus 30,000 (active peace establishment, SYB1913) = about 100,000 trained reservists. Because both inputs are approximate and come from different sources, this value is explicitly an estimate. SYB1913 gives no numerical reserve strength, only the reserve order of battle: 35 infantry regiments, 8 cavalry squadrons, 24 field batteries and other units; the territorial army had no cadres.
divergences: NYT1914's own figure is 130,000 for active + two reserves combined; if a user wants the total trained mobilisable manpower including the active army, use 130,000 instead of the 100,000 reserve-only estimate.
NYT1914 also mentions 'perhaps 50,000 men of the territorial reserve' — additional, largely untrained manpower, not included in the 100,000.

HCPT's war-planning figures (5 infantry divisions on outbreak, ultimately 12 more) imply far larger wartime mobilisation, consistent with the trained-reserve estimate but not usable as a January 1914 active figure.
SYB1913's liability rules (10 years active, 10 reserve, 5 territorial, ages 17-45) imply a much larger theoretical manpower pool; the source does not quantify it.

portugal.organisation: The Army of Portugal was a conscript militia. All males were liable from 17 to 45 (practically from 20): 10 years in the active army, 10 in the reserve, 5 in the territorial army (which also absorbed surplus men). Recruits underwent 15-30 weeks' preliminary training depending on arm, plus a fortnight's annual training. The country was divided into 3 territorial military districts (North, Centre, South), each expected to produce a division; each comprised two territorial divisions, and there were also the Azores and Madeira military commands plus the separate Lisbon Entrenched Camp command. The 1911 republican reform (January-May 1911) turned a largely professional army into a mainly militia army: the active troops comprised 8 divisions (each 4 infantry regiments, 1 machine-gun battery group, 1 mounted artillery regiment, 1 cavalry regiment) and a cavalry brigade of 3 regiments, plus non-divisional engineers, mountain/horse/howitzer artillery, 3 independent infantry regiments, machine-gun companies and services. In SYB terms: 35 infantry regiments of 3 battalions, 11 cavalry regiments of 4 squadrons, 8 field artillery regiments (63 batteries), 2 horse batteries, 9 mountain batteries, 20 garrison batteries and engineer units; batteries had 4 guns. Reserve army (cadres only in peace): 35 infantry regiments, 8 cavalry squadrons, 24 field batteries; territorial army had no cadres. Republican Guard ~5,000 (800 mounted) and Fiscal Guard ~5,200 were military-recruited civil corps usable in the field in war. Infantry arm: Mauser-Vergueiro 6.5 mm magazine rifle; field artillery rearming with 7.5 cm Schneider Canet guns. No general mobilisation before 1916.
portugal.garrisons: Metropolitan garrisons were spread among the three military districts and the Lisbon Entrenched Camp; the campaign/field organisation existed only on mobilisation (HCPT: 'In peace there is no divisional organisation'). Overseas: 2 line infantry regiments (2 battalions each) permanently stationed in the Azores and 1 at Madeira, with garrison artillery (1 battalion Madeira, 2 in the Azores). A separate Colonial Army garrisoned West Africa, Mozambique, India etc.: about 650 officers (partly seconded from the home army), about 2,500 European NCOs and men (volunteers) and about 7,000 native troops (compulsory) — roughly 10,150 total, consistent with HCPT's 'about 10,000 men in the colonies'. In August-October 1914 reinforcements (c.1,600 men to Angola, c.1,527 to Mozambique) were sent, but these are post-January-1914 movements.
uncertainties: The SYB1913 '30,000 men' active establishment may or may not include the ~2,800 officers; the 1914 unit structure from the 1911 reform is well attested but the exact peace-time headcount actually present is not.
The reserve figure (100,000) is a derived estimate from an October 1914 newspaper report of official estimates; the SYB gives only reserve order of battle, no strength. Treat as approximate.
The NYT headline figure of 130,000 applies to active plus two reserves combined after wastage — it is a mobilisation estimate, not a peace-time active strength.
The exact headquarters of the Centre Military District (Coimbra versus Lisbon) is not firmly established from the sources consulted.

HCPT (British intelligence summary) was accessible only as a search-index excerpt and its exact date is unverified; its broader 44,000 'with colours' figure should not be substituted for the SYB active establishment without qualification.
The 1913 edition of the SYB is the closest accessible contemporary publication; its military sections were still current in January 1914, but this is an inference rather than a 1914-dated return.

active.reference_date: 1909-1910 (closest documented pre-war peace establishment; used as proxy for January 1914)
active.definition: Peace establishment of the field army actually maintained under arms: 4,415 officers + 89,227 NCOs and men (18,920 horses excluded). Four army corps, the Dobrudja independent brigade and the separate cavalry division. This is the standing/peace force, not the mobilised army.
active.derivation: 4,415 + 89,227 = 93,642; directly stated component figures, no estimation beyond the sum. Horses excluded from headcount.
divergences: Spartacus Educational gives 'around 100,000 men' regular strength (SPARTACUS_RO) - compatible rounding.
1911 Britannica describes the field army on a war footing as 225,000 combatants; this is a wartime establishment, not a peacetime under-arms figure.
No exact January 1914 return was found; the 1909-10 figure is the nearest contemporary documented peace establishment.

reserves.reference_date: 1909-1910 (establishment target; explicitly not fully organised by 1910)
reserves.definition: Projected territorial militia (second section, citizens aged 30-36, mustering in spring for shooting practice and autumn manoeuvres), intended to add 100,000 men; included men who had completed ranks service and conscripts chosen by lot but not called to the field army. Additionally the Gloata (Landsturm) comprised all citizens aged 36-46 for home service only, not quantified in the source.
divergences: The 100,000 militia figure was an establishment target and was reported as not completely organised up to 1910; the actually trained reserve in January 1914 is uncertain and may have been lower.
If the 225,000 war-footing field army is compared with the 93,642 peace establishment, the implied field-army reserve increment is about 131,000 - a derived, not stated, figure.

Wartime mobilisation was far larger: c.330,000 in the 1913 Second Balkan War (WIKI_RO_ARMY) / c.400,000 (SPARTACUS_RO) and 658,088 in 1916 (WIKI_RO_CAMPAIGN); these include Landsturm and newly raised units, not just trained reservists.

romania.organisation: Conscription under the law of 1891 as modified in 1900 and 1908. Three sections: first section, men 21-30 in the field army and its reserves; second section, men 30-36 in the territorial militia; third section, men 36-46 in the Gloata (Landsturm) for home service only. In peace the field army comprised four complete army corps plus an independent brigade in the Dobrudja and a separate cavalry division. Infantry armed with Mannlicher M1893 magazine rifle, cavalry with Mannlicher carbine, horse and field artillery with Krupp quick-firing guns. War-footing field army 225,000 combatants; territorial system designed for rapid mobilisation and reinforcement from reserves.
romania.garrisons: Corps headquarters at Craiova, Bucharest, Jassy and Galatz; independent Dobrudja brigade; separate cavalry division at Bucharest. Fortifications designed by the Belgian general Brialmont: the Sereth Line from Galatz to Focshani (45 miles) and the fortified camp of Bucharest, plus works at Galatz and Focshani, armed with Krupp and Gruson guns. Main army depots and the Danube/Black Sea naval bases at Galatz and Constantza.
uncertainties: The exact January 1914 peace return has not been located; 1909-10 figures are the nearest reliable contemporary data.
The 100,000 militia figure was an unfulfilled target; actual trained reserve strength in January 1914 is an estimate at best.
The territorial organisation of 1912-1916 is documented in Romanian military literature that was not directly accessible here; corps HQ locations are from the 1911 Britannica.
Wartime mobilisation figures (1913, 1916, 1917) vary widely by source and are not interchangeable with peacetime or reserve figures.

active.definition: Peace strength of permanent troops, WITHOUT the annual contingent of recruits: 13,500 officers and men. Independently corroborated as the 'peace-time force of 13,500 men' on the eve of the August 1914 mobilisation. In addition, annual contingents of c.22,500 men trained 2-3 years with the colours and c.17,000 short-trained special reservists passed through the ranks, so the number actually under arms rose to c.60,000 on average and up to 75,000 at certain periods of the year.
active.derivation: Directly stated figure (13,500 officers and men), cross-checked against TANK_DK for August 1914. The annual contingents are counted as trained reserve/manning pool rather than the permanent active establishment.
divergences: GLOBALSEC_DK gives 'about 14,000 men and officers' - compatible rounding.
If the annual colour contingents are included, 'under arms' at peak training periods reached 75,000 (EB1911_DK) - a very different definition of 'active'.
TANK_DK records 47,000 under arms by 7 August 1914 and 58,000 by end-1914; these are post-mobilisation, not January 1914, figures.
Grokipedia-style claims of a c.50,000 peacetime army expandable to 120,000 are not supported by contemporary official statistics and are rejected.

reserves.definition: Reservists who had definitively left the colours and were recalled for short refresher training: c.80,000 in 1907. They supplement the annual contingent of c.22,500 long-trained men and c.17,000 special reservists. Term of service: 8 years in the active army and its reserves, then 8 years in the second line. A national militia system with very rare exemptions, somewhat on the Swiss model.
divergences: The 80,000 figure counts men given refresher training in one year, not necessarily the entire trained reserve pool; the true pool may have been somewhat larger.

Field army on a war footing was c.50,000 without depot/garrison troops and reservists; with reserves it could be more than doubled, and nearly 120,000 were with the colours in the 1907 manoeuvre season.
The post-mobilisation Sicherheitsmacht/Security Force reached c.47,000 in August 1914 and c.58,000-60,000 by late 1914.

denmark.organisation: Small conscript/militia army oriented to the defence of Copenhagen and the Danish Straits after the 1864 national trauma. Active army in 1911: one Life Guard battalion, 10 infantry regiments of 3 battalions, 5 cavalry regiments of 3 squadrons, 12 field batteries (Krupp QF), 3 fortress artillery battalions, 6 engineer companies plus local troops. Infantry armed with the Krag-Jørgensen M1889 (0.314 in); field artillery 7.5 cm Krupp QF M1902. Eight years active+reserve, eight years second line. On 1 August 1914 the army was mobilised as the Security Force (Sikringsstyrken) to guard neutrality; roughly 10,000 troops were posted on the Jutland-German border, the bulk around Copenhagen.
denmark.garrisons: Copenhagen/Zealand (capital, fortified position with the Vestvolden and north-front forts) was the main concentration; Jutland and Funen provided regional troops; Bornholm had a separate small garrison. Principal fortresses/strongpoints around Copenhagen and at the Danish Straits; the German frontier in southern Jutland was watched by a small covering force.
uncertainties: Danish territorial commands in 1914 are only indirectly documented here; district HQs are plausible garrison locations and should be treated as approximate.

Sources agree closely on the 13,500 permanent peace establishment, but 'troops under arms' can legitimately be read as 13,500, c.60,000 (annual average including recruits) or 75,000 (peak) depending on definition.
The 80,000 reservist figure is from 1907; January 1914 may have differed somewhat.

active.definition: Peace establishment of the line: 12,000 men with 750 officers. The only enlisted (long-service) troops were the fortress garrisons and the Christiania garrison of Norwegian Guards; the line was otherwise a cadre trained for 18-102 days per year. This is the force under arms in peacetime, distinct from the much larger total trained establishment (see divergences).
divergences: A later (c.1920) description quoted in WIKI_NO_ARMY gives a 'total peace strength' of 118,500 men with 71,836 rifles, 228 field and 36 heavy guns. This almost certainly denotes the total trained line+landværn establishment on paper, NOT troops continuously under arms, and is roughly ten times the peace establishment of the line.
The same source gives 282,000 additional men available on mobilisation, implying a theoretical wartime pool of roughly 400,000 - an establishment figure, not a peacetime presence.
EB1911_NO states a war footing of 26,000 or more but not exceeding 18,000 without parliamentary authority; this ambiguity is noted rather than resolved.

reserves.reference_date: c.1920 description of the system in force from 1911/1914 (approximate proxy for January 1914)
reserves.definition: Additional men available on mobilisation under the militia/territorial system: the landværn (reserve, 6 years) and landstorm (second reserve, 4 years), with war liability from 18 to 50 and 12 years in the line followed by 12 in the landvern then the landstorm. The figure is an establishment/pool estimate, NOT reservists under arms in peacetime.
divergences: The source text describes the post-1920 'national militia' organisation of a system introduced earlier; the exact January 1914 reserve total is uncertain.
EB1911_NO describes the same three-tier structure (line, landværn, landstorm) but gives no headcount for the reserves, only the line's war footing of 26,000.

The 118,500 'peace strength' and 282,000 mobilisable extras from the same later source should not be added to the 12,750 line peace establishment without triple-counting; they describe different levels of the same establishment.

norway.organisation: Militia/territorial-style conscription rather than a large standing army. Six brigades established in 1911 as district organisations, redesignated divisions by Army Order 1916; in 1914 they were still brigades. Each district was roughly a brigade (about four infantry battalions plus an artillery regiment) rather than a full division. Army order of c.1920: 56 infantry battalions, 5 cyclist/ski companies, 3 cavalry regiments (16 squadrons), 27 field batteries, 3 mountain batteries, 9 heavy artillery batteries, 1 engineer regiment and 2 battalions; a small flying corps. Initial training 48 days (infantry/garrison artillery) to 102 days (cavalry); 30 days additional training in the first year and 80 days in the 2nd, 3rd and 7th years. Norway stayed mobilised throughout the First World War to defend its neutrality.
norway.garrisons: Principal fortresses: Oscarsborg on Christiania Fjord, Agdenes at Trondhjem Fjord, Bergen, Tönsberg and Christiansand; Norwegian Guards garrison at Christiania. Forts on the Swedish frontier south of 61° N were dismantled under the 1905 convention with Sweden and a neutral zone created. Main district centres at Christiania, Bergen, Trondhjem, Stavanger/Christiansand and northern Norway.
uncertainties: The exact HQs of the six 1911-1914 brigade districts are not firmly documented in the sources consulted; the listed towns are plausible district centres.
The 118,500 / 282,000 figures come from a c.1920 description and may not apply unchanged to January 1914.
The difference between the 12,000-man line peace establishment (1911) and the later 118,500 'peace strength' is a definition problem that cannot be fully resolved from the accessible sources.
No dedicated US War Department 1916 handbook text was accessible; the 1911 Britannica was used instead.

active.definition: Permanent cadres about 22,000 officers, NCOs and specialists — the standing peacetime establishment around which the conscript army was trained. In addition c.85,000 men were trained annually as recruits or recalled for further training, so the number under arms at any one time fluctuated. Conscripts served 240 days (infantry, position/fortress artillery, fortress engineers, army service corps) or 365 days (cavalry, field artillery, field engineers, field telegraph) under the 1901 law.
active.derivation: Directly stated figure ('The permanent cadres number about 22,000'). No arithmetic derivation.
divergences: WIKI_SE_WW1 states the active strength of the Swedish army never exceeded 13,000 men during 1914-1918 - this appears to count active deployable field troops rather than the whole permanent cadre and training establishment.
The 1911 Britannica's c.85,000 men trained or recalled annually is a throughput figure, not a simultaneous under-arms headcount.
The NYT 1914 claim of a 350,000 'regular peace footing' is a grossly inflated contemporary press estimate and is rejected (see NYT_SE).

reserves.reference_date: 1911 (official estimate of total wartime manpower available)
reserves.definition: Estimated number of men available for service in the various capacities in case of war - the trained reserve pool under general conscription (ages 21-40: 8 years first levy, 4 years second levy, 8 years reserves). This is a theoretical mobilisable pool, not troops under arms in January 1914.
divergences: WIKI_SE_ARMY gives a consistent wartime army strength of about 100,000 men in the 1902-1939 period, two-thirds conscripts - a much narrower 'field army mobilised' definition than the 500,000 total available.
Hammarskjöld's 1914 Army Bill proposed doubling reserve formations from six to twelve infantry divisions and a cavalry division; this was a projected expansion, not an achieved January 1914 strength.

NYT_SE claimed a 'pure militia reserve of about 500,000' and nearly 900,000 under arms at twelve hours' notice - the 500,000 coincidentally matches the official estimate but the 900,000 total is unsupported wartime alarmism.

sweden.organisation: General conscription introduced in 1901-1902, replacing the old indelta (indelningsverket) system of military tenure every man between 21 and 40 served 8 years in the first levy, 4 in the second and 8 in the reserves. Peace organisation (1911): 82 infantry battalions in 28 regiments, 50 cavalry squadrons, 71 field artillery and 7 position artillery batteries, 10 fortress artillery companies, 16 engineer companies and 18 army service corps companies, grouped in six divisions plus the separate Gotland troops. A war division would probably comprise 4 infantry regiments (12 battalions), 4 cavalry squadrons, 1 artillery regiment, 1 engineer company etc.; a cavalry division 2 brigades of 8 squadrons plus horse artillery. Army Bill of 1914 proposed doubling reserve formations to twelve infantry divisions and a cavalry division. Sweden remained neutral throughout the war and its active deployable army declined from c.13,000 in 1914 to as few as 2,000 in 1918.
sweden.garrisons: Six division headquarters at Helsingborg, Linköping, Sköfde (Skövde), Stockholm (two divisions) and Hernösand (Härnösand), plus the Gotland troops at Visby. Fortresses: Stockholm with Vaxholm and Oscar-Fredriksborg, Boden near the Russian/Finnish frontier, Karlsborg on Lake Vetter, Karlskrona, plus forts at Gothenburg and on Gotland. The coastal artillery (Kustartilleriet, c.7,500 men in 1914) belonged to the Navy rather than the Army.
uncertainties: The 22,000 permanent cadres, c.85,000 trained annually, c.100,000 mobilised field army and c.500,000 total wartime availability are four different categories and must not be conflated.
The active deployable strength during the war (c.13,000 maximum, falling to 2,000) is from a later academic synthesis and may not equal the January 1914 peacetime under-arms figure.
Division HQ locations are from the 1911 Britannica and may have shifted slightly by 1914.
NYT 1914 mass-mobilisation claims are demonstrably inflated and are retained only as a documented divergence.
